texts.0: SP, due to reusing a flight plan form from a previous navigation sortie without rechecking it against the current route, did not fill the flight plan correctly and left route, endurance and alternate fields inconsistent with the planned mission. The plan was rejected at submission and the departure slot was lost. IP had to rewrite the flight plan and file it before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to copying the route from memory instead of from the plotted map, filled the flight plan with one turning point missing and with an endurance figure that did not match the computed fuel. Each incorrect field was corrected only after IP pointed to it in turn. The flight plan was brought to the lower limit of the standard by verbal prompting alone and was filed after the planned filing time.
texts.2: SP, due to transposing two turning points while completing the route field, first produced a flight plan that did not match the plotted track. SP detected the discrepancy during a self-check against the map, corrected the route, endurance and fuel entries and filed the plan on time. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP filled the flight plan completely and correctly, with route, cruising level, true airspeed, endurance, fuel and alternate all consistent with the plotted map and the computed data. The plan was filed within the time required by the Squadron Tactical Standards. No entry required correction.
texts.4: SP filled an exceptional flight plan, cross-checking every field against the plotted route, the performance computations and the current NOTAM before filing. Endurance, fuel and alternate entries were supported by figures SP had already computed for two loading cases. Departures from the ideal entry were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP filled and filed the flight plan within standards, but endurance and fuel were entered from a standard sortie figure rather than from the computation made for this route. The trend is toward a form that is formally correct while the numbers on it are not the numbers SP actually calculated. SP is expected to transfer computed values directly into the flight plan on the next sortie.

texts.0: SP, due to plotting the route by eye without using the plotter and the map scale, did not plot the route on the map correctly and produced tracks with course errors large enough to place two legs outside the intended corridor. Distances and drawn headings did not agree with the mission card. IP had to replot the whole route before the brief could start.
texts.1: SP, due to an inaccurate origin of the first leg, plotted the route with track angles that were consistently offset and with the ten-nautical-mile marks omitted on three legs. The plot was brought to an acceptable state only after IP indicated each leg that had to be redrawn. The map reached the lower limit of the standard and the planning phase overran the allotted time.
texts.2: SP, due to using an outdated map edition for the first plot, initially drew one leg through an area whose boundary had been amended. SP identified the discrepancy while checking the plot against the current chart, transferred the affected legs to the current edition and remeasured the tracks and distances in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP plotted the route on the map correctly, with tracks, distances and turning points measured accurately and marked clearly on the current chart edition. Leg distance marks and the safety altitude for each leg were annotated as required. The plot agreed with the mission card throughout.
texts.4: SP produced an exceptional route plot, with tracks and distances measured to the resolution of the plotter, and with turning points, distance marks, safety altitudes and airspace boundaries annotated so clearly that the map could be used without reference to any other document. Deviations from the ideal plot were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP plotted the route on the map within standards, but the annotation was crowded around the turning points and the leg distance marks were faint enough to be difficult to read in flight. The trend is toward a plot that is accurate on the ground but hard to use in the cockpit. SP is expected to plot with cockpit legibility in mind on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: PERFORMANCE CHART USE AND DATA COMPUTATION

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the Flight Manual performance charts, did not produce the takeoff, climb, enroute, descent and landing computations required for the mission. The figures presented were read from the wrong chart and the fuel required for the route was understated by a margin that would not have supported the alternate. IP had to recompute all the data before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to entering the climb chart with pressure altitude instead of density altitude, produced climb fuel and time figures that did not match the conditions of the day, and left the landing distance computation blank. The data set was completed only after IP identified each chart and each missing entry. The computations reached the lower limit of the standard and the planning phase ran well past the scheduled time.
texts.2: SP, due to an interpolation error between two chart lines, first computed an enroute fuel figure that did not agree with the leg times. SP noticed the inconsistency while cross-checking fuel against time, repeated the interpolation correctly and corrected the descent and landing figures in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP demonstrated good knowledge of the Flight Manual performance charts, the aeronautical maps and MAIP, and computed takeoff, climb, enroute, descent and landing data correctly for the conditions of the day. Interpolation was carried out accurately and the results were consistent with the leg times and the fuel plan. No computation required correction.
texts.4: SP demonstrated exceptional command of the performance charts, the aeronautical maps and MAIP, computing all phases for the actual conditions and additionally for a higher temperature and a heavier landing case. Every figure was traceable to a named chart and page and cross-checked against the fuel and time plan. Departures from the ideal computation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP computed all required performance data within standards, but every figure was taken to the nearest chart line without interpolation, and the takeoff and landing distances were therefore optimistic for the day. The trend is toward a data set that is complete but not precise enough to support a marginal runway. SP is expected to interpolate between chart lines and to state the assumptions used on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: SELECTION OF SIGNIFICANT GROUND REFERENCES PER LEG

texts.0: SP, due to selecting checkpoints from the map without considering how they would appear from the planned altitude, did not select significant ground references for the legs of the route and offered features that are not identifiable in flight. Two legs were left with no usable reference at all. IP had to select the checkpoints and rebuild the timing plan around them.
texts.1: SP, due to choosing linear features that lie along the track rather than across it, selected references that do not confirm position on three legs and omitted a reference for the leg with the longest overwater segment. Usable checkpoints were selected only after IP prompted for each leg in turn. The selection reached the lower limit of the standard and delayed completion of the mission card.
texts.2: SP, due to selecting an initial checkpoint that would be behind the wing at the planned flight altitude, first produced a reference for the second leg that could not be seen from the cockpit. SP recognized the problem while reviewing the legs against the planned altitude, replaced it with a distinct road and lake intersection and adjusted the leg times accordingly, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP selected significant ground references for every leg of the route, choosing features that are large, unique and identifiable from the planned flight altitude. Each reference was marked on the map with its time and distance from the turning point. The selection supported position confirmation throughout the route.
texts.4: SP selected exceptional ground references, with a primary and a secondary feature for each leg, chosen for contrast against the surrounding terrain and for visibility in the expected haze and sun angle. Each reference carried its time, distance and expected relative position. Departures from the ideal selection were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP selected significant ground references for every leg within standards, but the choices were concentrated near the turning points, leaving long stretches of each leg without a position check. The trend is toward a route that can be flown but not continuously verified. SP is expected to distribute the references along the whole leg on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: MISSION CARD COMPLETION AND USE OF AERONAUTICAL PUBLICATIONS

texts.0: SP, due to preparing the mission card from a previous sortie without consulting MAIP, the maps, the FLIPs and the Flight Manual, filled it with omissions in headings, leg times, fuel and frequencies. Several entries contradicted the plotted route and no reference was made to AFMAN 11-202 Vol 3 or to the Flight Procedures manual. IP had to rebuild the card before the brief.
texts.1: SP, due to transcribing frequencies and field data from memory rather than from the current publications, left the alternate airfield block and two leg fuel entries empty on the mission card. Each omission was filled only after IP pointed to it. The card reached the lower limit of the standard and was completed after the scheduled start of the briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to using a superseded MAIP page for the destination, initially entered a tower frequency that had been amended. SP identified the discrepancy while cross-checking the card against the current publication, corrected the frequency and rechecked the remaining field data in good time. The card was completed without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP filled the mission card correctly and without omissions, using MAIP, the maps, the FLIPs, the Flight Manual, AFMAN 11-202 Vol 3 and the Flight Procedures manual. Headings, distances, leg times, fuel, frequencies and field data agreed with the plotted route and the computed performance data. No entry required correction.
texts.4: SP filled an exceptional mission card, complete, legible and ordered for cockpit use, with every entry traceable to the current publication it came from. Field data, frequencies and fuel figures were cross-checked twice and the card was usable without reference to any other document in flight. Departures from the ideal card were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP filled the mission card without omissions and within standards, but the handwriting and the column layout make the fuel and time blocks difficult to read in the cockpit at low light. The trend is toward a card that is technically complete but slow to use in flight. SP is expected to produce a card that can be read at a glance on the next sortie.

texts.0: SP, due to preparing the briefing without following the Squadron Tactical Standards briefing sequence, did not execute the briefing without omissions and left out the route review, the weather and the emergency section entirely. The objectives of the sortie were never stated. IP had to stop the briefing, take it over and rebrief the whole profile.
texts.1: SP, due to briefing from the mission card instead of from a prepared flow, omitted the airspace restrictions and the abort criteria and covered the alternate airfields only when asked directly. Each missing paragraph was delivered only after IP prompted for it. The briefing reached the lower limit of the standard and ran about fifteen minutes over the scheduled time.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the briefing out of sequence, initially passed over the weather and NOTAM review before the route description. SP recognized the omission, returned to it and completed the remaining paragraphs in the correct order and inside the scheduled time. The briefing was completed to standard without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the briefing without omissions, covering objectives, route, altitudes, ground references, timings, fuel, weather, NOTAM, airspace restrictions, alternate airfields and emergency procedures in the prescribed sequence. The briefing was delivered inside the time allotted and each item was tied to the plan on the map and the mission card. No paragraph required prompting.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional briefing, delivering every paragraph from a prepared flow, with the threats for the day identified and a mitigation stated for each. Contingencies raised during the briefing were already supported by figures SP had computed in advance. Departures from the ideal briefing were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the briefing without omissions and within standards, but the delivery was a recitation of headings with little reference to the actual weather, runway and airspace situation of the day. The trend is toward a briefing that covers the required items without converting them into decisions for this sortie. SP is expected to brief each item against the actual conditions on the next event.

texts.0: SP, due to absent inquiry into events that had already been contradicted by the recorded times and fuel, did not execute the debriefing and could not reconstruct the sequence of the sortie. Errors on the route were neither identified nor attributed to a cause, and no corrective technique was proposed. IP had to conduct the entire debriefing and state the findings for SP.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to question an assumption about the position fix at the second turning point, debriefed the sortie chronologically without isolating the cause of the track error and omitted the fuel and timing analysis. Each finding emerged only after IP asked a direct question. The debriefing reached the lower limit of the standard and no corrective action was proposed by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to no advocacy of an alternative explanation once the first reconstruction of the leg had clearly failed, initially attributed the timing error to the forecast wind. SP re-examined the recorded headings, identified the actual cause as a late turn at the second turning point and proposed the corrective technique without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the debriefing without omissions, reconstructing the sortie against the mission card, identifying each deviation, attributing it to a cause and proposing a corrective technique. Fuel, timings and track keeping were analysed against the plan. The debriefing was completed within the time allotted and no finding had to be supplied by IP.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional debriefing, reconstructing the sortie leg by leg with times, fuel and headings, separating planning errors from execution errors, and proposing a specific corrective technique and a measurable objective for the next sortie. Every conclusion was supported by recorded data. Departures from the ideal debriefing were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the debriefing within standards, but the analysis stopped at describing what happened and reached the underlying cause only for the most obvious deviation. The trend is toward a debriefing that records events without converting them into training objectives. SP is expected to state a cause and a corrective technique for every deviation on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: ALTERNATE AIRFIELD SELECTION AND TURNING POINT DIVERT DATA

texts.0: SP, due to the absence of explicit divert criteria in the mission plan, did not choose alternate airfields and did not plan heading, time and fuel to the nearest airfield from any turning point. The route was planned as if recovery to the departure field were assured. IP had to select the alternates and compute the divert data before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to no named decision point for the weather deterioration that had been forecast, selected one alternate for the whole route and computed divert heading, time and fuel for only the first two turning points. The remaining turning points were covered only after IP asked for each in turn. The divert plan reached the lower limit of the standard and was completed after the scheduled brief time.
texts.2: SP, due to a briefed decision point that was first left without a fuel figure attached to it, initially produced divert data that could not be used to make the decision in flight. SP identified the gap while reviewing the mission card, computed the fuel required from that turning point to the nearest airfield and attached it to the decision point, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP chose suitable alternate airfields for the route and planned heading, time and fuel from every turning point to the nearest airfield, computed within logical error and entered on the mission card. Field data and frequencies for each alternate were taken from the current publications. The divert plan was usable in flight without further computation.
texts.4: SP chose exceptional alternates and produced divert heading, time and fuel from every turning point for two fuel states, with a named decision point and a stated criterion attached to each leg. The data were laid out on the mission card so that the divert decision could be made in flight in a single reading. Departures from the ideal plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP selected alternate airfields and computed divert data for every turning point within standards, but the fuel figures carry no allowance for a missed approach at the alternate. The trend is toward a divert plan that works only if the first approach at the alternate succeeds. SP is expected to build a usable reserve into the divert figures on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: WEATHER, NOTAM AND OPERATIONAL RESTRICTIONS REVIEW

texts.0: SP, due to a threat present in the minimum threat set but not identified during planning, did not review the weather, the NOTAM and the airspace restrictions for the route and planned a leg through an active restricted area. The VMC minima for the day were never checked against the forecast. IP had to stop the planning, produce the restrictions and rebuild the affected legs.
texts.1: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, reviewed the departure field weather only and omitted the enroute NOTAM for the second half of the route. The restrictions were identified only after IP directed SP to each publication in turn. The review reached the lower limit of the standard and the flight plan was filed late as a result.
texts.2: SP, due to a currency shortfall in the NOTAM briefing that was not addressed at the start of the planning phase, initially planned a leg at an altitude affected by a temporary restriction. SP identified the restriction while completing the second check of the route, replanned the leg altitude and adjusted the fuel and time figures, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP reviewed the weather, the NOTAM, the airspace restrictions and the flight plan requirements for the whole route and confirmed that the day only VFR and VMC conditions of the sortie were satisfied. Each identified threat was carried into the plan with a stated mitigation. No restriction had to be produced by IP.
texts.4: SP reviewed the weather, NOTAM and restrictions exceptionally, tracking the forecast trend across the planned recovery window and identifying every threat on the route together with the decision point at which it would be managed. The alternates were selected against the same forecast trend. Departures from the ideal review were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP reviewed the weather, NOTAM and restrictions within standards, but the review was recorded as a list of items checked rather than as threats carried into the plan. The trend is toward information that is collected but not converted into a mitigation or a decision point. SP is expected to state the mitigation for each identified threat on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: FORMATION SORTIE PLANNING AND BRIEFING ITEMS (N44XX / N45XX)

texts.0: SP, due to planning the N44XX and N45XX sortie as a single ship navigation, did not apply the corresponding formation items and left the join up, the formation position changes, the lost wingman procedure and the visual signals out of the plan and the brief. The formation recovery was never addressed. IP had to plan and brief the formation items in full.
texts.1: SP, due to using a single ship briefing flow for a formation navigation sortie, omitted the lost wingman procedure and the formation breakup from the brief and covered the visual signals only in outline. Each formation item was briefed only after IP prompted for it. The plan and the brief reached the lower limit of the standard and delayed step in.
texts.2: SP, due to an omission of the formation breakup point in the first version of the plan, initially briefed a recovery that did not state where the elements would separate. SP identified the gap while reviewing the route with the map, added the breakup point with its fuel and time figures and briefed it in sequence, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP applied the corresponding formation items to the N44XX and N45XX sortie, planning and briefing join up, formation positions and changes, visual signals, lost wingman, formation breakup and recovery as described for formation sorties. The formation items were integrated with the route, fuel and timing plan. No item required prompting.
texts.4: SP applied the formation items exceptionally, planning and briefing every N44XX and N45XX requirement with the responsibilities of lead and wing stated for each phase, and with the lost wingman and breakup contingencies supported by computed fuel and time figures. The formation plan and the navigation plan were fully consistent. Departures from the ideal were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP applied the corresponding formation items within standards, but the responsibilities for navigation and lookout between lead and wing were briefed in general terms rather than allocated by phase. The trend is toward a formation plan that states the procedure without assigning who does what. SP is expected to allocate navigation and lookout duties explicitly on the next formation navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: CHART MARKING DISCIPLINE AND DATA BOX PLACEMENT
error_modes.source: technique:8.18.3 CHART PREPARATION - CHECKPOINTS, COURSE LINE, MAGNETIC COURSE, DISTANCE, TIMING TICS

texts.0: SP, due to marking the chart without the general rule to minimize marking up the chart, ran the course lines straight through the checkpoint circles and placed the data boxes over geographical features usable for navigation. Three checkpoints could not be read under the ink and the leg data had to be recovered from the mission card. IP had to prepare a new chart before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to inking the route before the plot was complete, could not correct the course lines that had been carried through the checkpoint circles and left two data boxes covering usable terrain. The chart was made serviceable only after IP indicated each obscured checkpoint and each misplaced box. Chart preparation reached the lower limit of the standard and the planning phase overran the allotted time.
texts.2: SP, due to placing the first data box over a coastline used as a leg reference, initially obscured a feature usable for navigation. SP noticed the conflict while checking the chart against the checkpoint list, erased the box and redrew it along the direction of the leg and clear of the terrain. The remaining boxes and course lines were then positioned correctly in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP prepared the chart with marking kept to the minimum required, stopping each course line at the edge of the checkpoint circle so that the data over the checkpoint was not obscured. Each data box was drawn along the segment, pointing in the direction the leg is to be flown, and clear of any geographical feature usable for navigation. All marks were made in pencil first and inked only after the work was complete. No annotation obscured needed information.
texts.4: SP prepared an exceptional chart, with every course line stopped exactly at the circle edge, every data box aligned with the direction of flight and placed over featureless ground or sea, and the whole route legible at arm's length in the cockpit. Pencil work was completed and checked before any ink was applied, so late changes to the route cost nothing. Departures from the ideal chart were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP prepared the chart within standards, with course lines stopped at the circles and no usable terrain obscured, but the whole route was inked before the timing and fuel figures were finalized. The trend is toward a chart that cannot absorb a change of route or of checkpoint without being redrawn. SP is expected to keep the chart in pencil until the plan is fixed on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: DESTINATION AND ROUTE SELECTION RULES OF THUMB

texts.0: SP, due to selecting a destination and a route without the 200 to 300 NM rule of thumb and without coordinating either with the instructor, built a route that left no fuel reserve for practice approaches and patterns at the destination. The route carried three checkpoints instead of the minimum of six to eight, so long stretches offered no means of confirming position. IP had to reselect the destination and rebuild the route before planning could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to fixing the destination late and starting the route work before it was established, presented four checkpoints and a total distance well outside the 200 to 300 NM band, with no fuel computed for diverting to the alternates along the route. Each missing checkpoint and each missing fuel figure was added only after IP named it. Route selection reached the lower limit of the standard and pushed chart preparation past the scheduled time.
texts.2: SP, due to a route whose second leg placed the checkpoints more than 25 minutes apart, first produced a plan with a long unmonitored stretch. SP identified it while counting the checkpoints against the six to eight minimum, inserted two prominent points and recomputed the affected leg times and fuel. The destination and the amended route were coordinated with the instructor before chart preparation began, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP selected a destination within approximately 200 to 300 NM of the departure airport and a route carrying six to eight checkpoints, and coordinated both with the instructor before beginning flight planning. Fuel was planned for diverting to alternates along the entire route, for bingo, for completing the mission as briefed and for the emergency requirement. Terminal forecasts for homefield and destination were obtained as soon as the destination was established. No element of the selection required correction.
texts.4: SP selected an exceptional destination and route, with distance, checkpoint count and spacing all inside the rules of thumb and with an alternative routing already prepared against the forecast weather. Fuel was planned for diverts, bingo, mission completion and the emergency requirement, and the route was obtained early enough for unhurried chart preparation. Departures from the ideal selection were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP selected destination and route within standards, but the choice was driven by distance alone and the forecast weather for the return flight was reviewed only after the route had been fixed. The trend is toward a route that is correct on paper and vulnerable to the weather of the day. SP is expected to weigh weather first and distance second when selecting the next route.

error_modes.label: ROUTE TIMING CHAIN AND TIME ON TARGET
error_modes.source: technique:8.18.3.h-i TIME OVER TARGET (TOT) AND ROUTE TIMING

texts.0: SP, due to computing each leg time in isolation instead of building the elapsed time chain from a 0+00 hack in the first data box, did not produce a timing plan and left the final checkpoint without a Time On Target. Leg times were figured at a speed other than the planning 210 knots ground speed, so no total agreed with the planned time enroute. IP had to rebuild the timing for the whole route.
texts.1: SP, due to adding each leg time to the wrong preceding entry, produced an elapsed time chain in which the final checkpoint did not equal the total pre-planned time enroute, and left the two minute tic marks off two legs. The chain was corrected only after IP identified each data box to be recomputed. Timing reached the lower limit of the standard and no hard arrival times were available for the brief.
texts.2: SP, due to using 3.0 miles per minute instead of the planning figure of 3.5 miles per minute on the first leg, initially entered an elapsed time that did not match the measured leg distance. SP found the discrepancy while verifying that the last checkpoint equalled the total planned time enroute, recomputed the affected legs and reissued the hard times. The correction was made in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP built the timing from a 0+00 hack in the bottom of the first data box, added each leg time computed at 210 knots ground speed to the previous elapsed time and verified that the final checkpoint equalled the total pre-planned time enroute. Checkpoints were sequentially numbered and hard arrival times were determined in advance from the intended route commencement time. SP stated the 60 to 1 correction, 10 knots of ground speed for 3.5 minutes per ten seconds of error, as the method for regaining timing. No entry required correction.
texts.4: SP built an exceptional timing plan, with the elapsed time chain verified against the Time On Target and a second set of hard times prepared for a delayed route commencement. Ground speed corrections were tabulated in advance from the 60 to 1 rule for errors of ten, twenty and forty seconds, so no computation would be required in flight. Departures from the ideal timing plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP built the timing chain within standards and the Time On Target agreed with the total planned time enroute, but the method briefed for correcting timing in flight was to cut off or extend the route. The trend is toward a plan whose only recovery from a timing error changes the planned track. SP is expected to brief ground speed corrections based on the 60 to 1 rule on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: CONTINUATION FUEL COMPUTED BACKWARDS ALONG THE ROUTE

texts.0: SP, due to computing fuel forward from takeoff instead of working backwards along the route of flight, produced no continuation fuel figure for any checkpoint and left the plan with no minimum fuel required at any point to complete the route with reserves. The final checkpoint was not the destination airport and the fuel to transit from the end of the route to the landing destination was never planned. IP had to compute continuation fuel for every leg before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting the local SOP reserves from the starting figure, produced continuation fuel values that were low on every leg and stopped the computation at the final checkpoint without adding the transit to the landing destination. Each leg was recomputed only after IP indicated the missing reserve and the missing transit. Fuel planning reached the lower limit of the standard and the brief started late.
texts.2: SP, due to an arithmetic slip while adding the second leg back towards takeoff, initially carried a continuation fuel figure that was inconsistent with the remaining fuel column of the navigation card. SP found it while cross-checking the data boxes against the card, repeated the backwards computation from the landing destination and corrected the affected boxes. The correction was completed in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP computed continuation fuel by working backwards along the route, starting from the local SOP reserves added to the fuel required to transit from the landing destination to the final checkpoint, then adding the fuel for each leg back to the initial takeoff. The figure was entered in the data box of every leg and on the navigation card, together with the bingo point. SP briefed that modification of the route, or terminating it early and proceeding direct to the final checkpoint, is the expected action if continuation fuel would be exceeded. No figure required correction.
texts.4: SP computed an exceptional continuation fuel plan, working backwards from the landing destination with the SOP reserves and stating for each checkpoint the fuel at which the route would be modified and the fuel at which it would be terminated. The figures were cross-checked against the leg times and against the divert data, and the case where the final checkpoint is not the destination airport was carried explicitly. Departures from the ideal computation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP computed continuation fuel for every checkpoint within standards, but the figures were presented as reference numbers with no stated action if they were not met in flight. The trend is toward a fuel plan that measures the situation without defining the decision. SP is expected to state the route modification or termination associated with each continuation fuel figure on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE PER LEG AND DATA BOX CONTENT

texts.0: SP, due to reading spot elevations only along the course line instead of taking the highest top inside the 5 NM buffer zone, entered minimum safe altitudes that did not clear the terrain either side of two legs and omitted the 500 foot addition altogether. The turn point numbers and the leg magnetic headings were also left out of the boxes. IP had to recompute the safety altitudes and complete the data boxes for the whole route.
texts.1: SP, due to rounding the highest top down instead of to the nearest hundred feet before adding 500 feet, entered minimum safe altitudes that were low on three legs, and left the continuation fuel field of two boxes empty. Each figure was corrected only after IP pointed to the leg concerned. The data boxes reached the lower limit of the standard and the planning phase overran.
texts.2: SP, due to applying the buffer zone to one side of the course line only, initially computed a minimum safe altitude that ignored a ridge inside the 5 NM buffer on the opposite side. SP detected it while comparing the leg against the chart contours, recomputed from the highest top in the full buffer, rounded to the nearest hundred and added 500 feet. The affected boxes and the navigation card were corrected without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP completed every data box with turn point number, leg magnetic heading corrected per the chart legend, leg length, leg time, minimum safe altitude and continuation fuel. Each minimum safe altitude was derived from the highest top inside the 5 NM buffer zone, rounded to the nearest hundred feet and increased by 500 feet, and agreed with the safety altitude column of the navigation card. No field required correction.
texts.4: SP completed the data boxes exceptionally, with every field filled and every minimum safe altitude traceable to the named high point inside the 5 NM buffer zone, rounded and increased by 500 feet, and cross-checked against the route abort altitude on the navigation card. The boxes were legible at a glance and consistent with the chart and the card throughout. Departures from the ideal were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the data boxes within standards and the minimum safe altitudes were correctly derived, but a single highest figure was carried across three adjacent legs rather than computed leg by leg. The trend is toward a safety altitude that is conservative in the aggregate and unrelated to the terrain of the individual leg. SP is expected to compute the minimum safe altitude separately for each leg on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: AIRSPACE ANNOTATION AND EMERGENCY AIRFIELD DIVERSION LINES
error_modes.source: technique:8.18.3.m-n AIRSPACE ANNOTATION AND EMERGENCY AIRFIELDS (DIVERSION LINES)

texts.0: SP, due to preparing the chart without the airspace annotation step, left the MTMAs, TMAs, LGDs and LGRs, the bird corridors and the bird concentration areas unmarked and selected no emergency airfields along the route. No diversion lines were drawn, so no landing area was identified for an abnormal situation on any leg. IP had to annotate the airspace and select the emergency airfields before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to annotating the chart from memory rather than from the current publications, highlighted the TMAs without their vertical limits, left two restricted areas unmarked and drew diversion lines of arbitrary length to only one emergency airfield. Each omission was completed after IP identified it on the chart. The annotation reached the lower limit of the standard and delayed the brief.
texts.2: SP, due to selecting the emergency airfield nearest to the departure field rather than applying the bisector between the two closest suitable fields, initially annotated a change of emergency airfield at the wrong point on the route. SP identified the error while checking the leg against the two candidate fields, moved the change point to the bisector intersection and redrew the 10 NM diversion lines. The chart was corrected without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP annotated the chart completely, with TMAs and MTMAs highlighted in blue and the ATZs, CTRs, dangerous and restricted areas in red with their names and vertical limits, bird corridors in green and bird concentration areas in red. Emergency airfields were selected along the route by joining the two closest suitable fields and taking the bisector to find where it intersects the route, and 10 NM diversion lines were drawn in red. The annotation agreed with the current publications throughout.
texts.4: SP produced an exceptional annotation, with every airspace boundary, vertical limit, bird corridor and concentration area colour coded as prescribed and every emergency airfield selected by the bisector method and marked with a 10 NM diversion line. Field elevation, runway and frequency for each emergency airfield were carried on the navigation card as well as on the chart. Departures from the ideal annotation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP annotated the airspace and drew the emergency airfield diversion lines within standards, but the annotation was so dense around two turning points that the underlying detail was hard to read. The trend is toward a chart that carries all the required information in a form that is slow to use in flight. SP is expected to keep the annotation legible over the checkpoints on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: MISSION SPECIFIC STUDY AND CHAIR FLYING

texts.0: SP, due to omitting mission specific study and chair flying, could not describe the manoeuvres to be flown, the local area procedures or the operational restrictions for this type of sortie. The approach plates for the destination and the emergency procedure of the day had not been reviewed and the checklists could not be recalled in sequence. IP had to conduct the study with SP before the mission could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to studying only the general subject areas and not the manoeuvres of this profile, could not state the entry parameters for two manoeuvres and had not reviewed the approach plates for the destination. Each item was covered only after IP prompted for it in turn. Preparation reached the lower limit of the standard and the briefing started late.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating the study on the primary mission alone, initially could not state the profile of the possible alternate mission. SP recognised the gap while reviewing the schedule, studied the alternate profile and chair flew its manoeuvres before the brief. Both profiles were then presented without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP completed mission specific study, reviewing the operational restrictions for the sortie, the approach plates, the local area procedures and each manoeuvre in the flight manual and in the techniques manual, and covered the daily study topics including the emergency procedure of the day. SP chair flew the sortie, visualizing the manoeuvres and techniques and mentally reviewing the checklists and specific tasks. Time was also devoted to the possible alternate mission. No area required prompting.
texts.4: SP completed exceptional mission specific study, chair flying the whole profile including the transitions between manoeuvres and the recovery, and reviewing the alternate mission to the same depth as the primary. Every manoeuvre could be described with its entry parameters and its common errors, and the emergency procedure of the day was demonstrated by flow. Departures from the ideal preparation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the mission specific study within standards, but the chair flying was a recital of checklist items rather than a visualization of the manoeuvres and the techniques. The trend is toward preparation that reproduces the sequence without rehearsing the flying. SP is expected to visualize each manoeuvre and its technique during chair flying on the next sortie.

texts.0: SP, due to treating the Go/No-Go items as a formality of the squadron routine, did not sign off the flight crew information file and the read files before flying, did not reserve the airspace required for the route and did not call the destination airfield. The local restrictions in force were unknown to SP at the brief. IP had to stop the preparation, complete the Go/No-Go items and arrange the airspace before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the administrative tasks until after the planning was finished, arrived at the brief with the read files unsigned and with no confirmation that the airspace had been reserved. Both were completed only after IP listed the outstanding items. The preparation reached the lower limit of the standard and the step time was put back.
texts.2: SP, due to overlooking the bird hazard model for the planned period, initially presented a route timing that placed two legs in a raised bird condition. SP identified it while reviewing the local restrictions, checked the model, shifted the route commencement and confirmed that the airspace booking still held. The plan was corrected in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP completed the planning administration in full, signing off the Go/No-Go items including the flight crew information file and the read files, checking the local profile and call sign, reserving the airspace required by the route and calling the destination airfield. The bird hazard model and the local restrictions in force were reviewed and carried into the plan. Every administrative task was complete before the briefing began.
texts.4: SP completed the planning administration exceptionally, with the Go/No-Go items signed off early, the airspace and the destination coordinated well before the brief, and the bird hazard model and local restrictions reviewed for both the planned and the alternate route. The results were presented as decisions affecting the plan rather than as items checked. Departures from the ideal preparation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the Go/No-Go items and the administrative tasks within standards, but the read files were signed immediately before the brief with no time to absorb their content. The trend is toward a signature that records compliance without the knowledge it is meant to certify. SP is expected to read and sign the required files well before the briefing on the next sortie.
